Hard Times. Serialized in 1854, this is Charles Dickens's shortest novel and his only explicitly political one. It is set in the industrial town of Coketown and launches an attack on utilitarian philosophy and industrial capitalism. The novel centers on Thomas Gradgrind, a schoolmaster and entrepreneur whose personal philosophy is captured in a single sentence: "Now, what I want is Facts." He believes education should consist entirely of facts, with no room for imagination, feeling, or fancy. His system crushes the souls of those around him, including his own children. Against Gradgrind stands Sissy Jupe, the daughter of a circus performer. She represents imagination, human warmth, and everything that Gradgrind's philosophy denies. She becomes the moral center of the entire novel. Louisa Gradgrind, the schoolmaster's own daughter, becomes a tragic emblem of Victorian female sacrifice. She is married off to the utilitarian industrialist Josiah Bounderby, in keeping with her father's cold principles. Bounderby is a pompous braggart who embodies capitalist self-deception and the callous abuse of workers. But the moral heart of the novel lies with Stephen Blackpool, a mill worker whose suffering at the hands of an indifferent system drives home Dickens's critique. Stephen experiences exploitation, injustice, and complete social abandonment. His tragedy shows the moral bankruptcy of systems that view human beings merely as productive units. Though it is Dickens's shortest major novel, it is written with pointed anger at Benthamite utilitarianism and the dehumanization wrought by the industrial age.
